note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Painful, cracked, itchy skin on palms of both hands.
  - Occupational exposure to cleaning products; inconsistent glove use. New hotel housekeeping job started ~3–4 months ago.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Onset ~3–4 months ago; progressively worsened. Now painful enough to impair work (off work past 3 days).
- ENT symptoms (as applicable):
  - Throat swelling/closure sensation: Not reported.
  - Voice change/hoarseness: Not reported.
  - Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling: Not reported.
  - Nasal/ocular symptoms: Not reported.
  - Stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea: Not reported.
  - Facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling: Not reported.
  - Ear/neck symptoms: Not reported.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  - No prior skin diagnoses noted.
  - Tried OTC emollient (E45) without benefit; tried an oral antihistamine without benefit (names/doses not documented).
  - No prior ED/hospital care or injection therapy.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergies: Denies medication or general allergies.
  - Current meds: Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Recent OTC: E45 emollient; antihistamine (names/dose/frequency not documented).
- Any relevant social context:
  - Works as a hotel housekeeper (bedrooms, bathrooms, corridors). Nonsmoker; minimal alcohol (“a couple of pints a week”). Not consistently wearing gloves; believes symptoms may relate to cleaning agents. Off work for 3 days due to pain.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution:
  - Not recorded (tele-visit; no visual exam documented).
- Airway/breathing descriptors:
  - Not recorded; no airway complaints reported.
- Mental status and associated features:
  - Feels otherwise well; denies fever, GI, urinary symptoms; appetite intact.
- Vitals and examination findings:
  - Not recorded.
- Presence of another person with the patient:
  - Not stated.

Assessment:
- Working clinical impression: Occupational irritant contact hand dermatitis, likely related to wet work and cleaning chemicals; chronic course with fissuring and pain. Xerosis may be contributory.
- Evidence summary:
  - Strong temporal association with new housekeeping job and frequent exposure to cleaning products; inconsistent glove use.
  - Palmar-dominant dryness, cracking, pain, intermittent itch; occasional bleeding only with scratching.
  - Lack of response to emollient and antihistamine; otherwise systemically well.
  - Type 2 diabetes may contribute to xerosis and impaired barrier repair.
- DDx (aligned with transcript):
  1) Irritant contact dermatitis (high likelihood): Classic occupational exposure pattern, palmar fissuring, onset after job change; antihistamine ineffective.
  2) Allergic contact dermatitis to occupational agents (medium likelihood): Potential sensitizers in cleaning products or gloves; pruritic hand dermatitis; opposing evidence—no clear specific trigger identified, timing soon after job change.
  3) Asteatotic/xerotic eczema (medium likelihood): Baseline generalized dryness and diabetes; opposing evidence—localization to palms and strong occupational link favor contact dermatitis.
- Conflict noted:
  - None between transcript and DDx.

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised:
  - Prescription to pharmacy: Topical corticosteroid cream/ointment for hands (specific agent/potency/directions not documented in transcript).
  - Stronger emollient prescribed; instructed to apply liberally 3–4 times daily for the next 10–14 days.
  - Strict avoidance of triggers: Wear protective gloves at all times when cleaning.
- Patient/caregiver instructions:
  - Maintain regular emollient use even after improvement to support skin barrier.
  - Minimize wet work and harsh soaps; rinse and dry hands thoroughly after exposure.
- Escalation criteria/red flags:
  - Seek care promptly if worsening pain, spreading rash, new blistering, signs of infection (increasing redness, warmth, swelling, purulent drainage, fever), or inability to perform activities due to pain.
- Follow-up:
  - Reassess in 10–14 days; return sooner if worsening or spreading.
  - If inadequate response, consider alternative diagnoses (e.g., allergic contact dermatitis) and referral for dermatology/occupational medicine evaluation and possible patch testing.
  - Continue diabetes management as prescribed; good glycemic control may aid skin healing.
- COVID-19 vaccine suitability:
  - Not discussed.

Quality checks:
● Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No visual exam findings (erythema, scaling pattern, distribution including dorsal hands/interdigital spaces) or vitals recorded.
  - Specific topical steroid agent, potency, dosing schedule, and duration not documented.
  - Emollient product and regimen beyond “3–4 times daily” not specified.
  - No documentation of secondary infection assessment, presence/absence of vesicles, or nail/foot involvement (to screen for tinea).
  - No occupational details about specific products/glove materials; no patch testing history.
  - No atopic history beyond asthma; allergic rhinitis/atopic dermatitis history not elicited.
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None noted.
● Transcript quality:
  - Generally clear; minor inaudible/unfinished phrases but core history understandable.
